task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper news story for general readers. Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of January 30, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: A study published January 30, 2025, in the journal Environmental Science Reports found microplastic particles in 89% of tap water samples collected from 1,200 households across 38 U.S. states.
The study detected particles at concentrations ranging from 12 to 930 particles per liter; the median concentration was 74 particles per liter.

Lead researcher Dr. Yolanda Kimura of the National Freshwater Institute said: "Microplastics are in the water supply more broadly than previous spot surveys suggested. What we do not yet know is what, if any, health consequence follows from chronic low-level ingestion."
No regulatory limit for microplastics in drinking water currently exists in the United States; the Environmental Protection Agency has listed microplastics as a research priority since 2022.

The study found no statistically significant difference in concentration between water treated by large municipal systems and water from small community wells, a result the authors described as unexpected.
Samples with the highest concentrations came from households using plastic plumbing supply lines installed after 2010; the study found a correlation but did not establish a causal mechanism.

Toxicologist Dr. Francis Lind, not affiliated with the study, said the health evidence for microplastics in drinking water remains inconclusive: "Animal studies suggest effects at high concentrations, but human epidemiological data is still limited. That gap needs to close before we can establish a standard."
The particles detected were predominantly polyethylene and polypropylene, consistent with plumbing and packaging sources.
Reverse osmosis filters removed more than 95% of detected particles in laboratory testing; standard carbon-block filters removed approximately 60%.
The study collected samples in spring and autumn over two years from 2022 to 2024.
Eleven of the 1,200 sampled households used well water without any municipal treatment; all 11 showed detectable microplastic levels.

The highest individual sample, 930 particles per liter, came from a household connected to a large municipal system in the Northeast; the study's authors noted this was an outlier and did not indicate that region had systematically elevated levels.
The EPA said it would review the study as part of its ongoing microplastics research program and expected to publish a risk assessment framework by 2027.
Bottled water was not included in the study; prior published research has found comparable or higher microplastic concentrations in bottled water.
The National Freshwater Institute received funding from the EPA and two environmental foundations; no industry funding was disclosed.

Dr. Kimura said the study's detection method uses infrared spectroscopy to identify plastic polymer types; earlier studies relied on visual identification, which may have undercounted smaller particles.
The 89% detection rate is higher than a 2021 European study that found microplastics in 72% of sampled tap water in eight countries.

Dr. Lind said the priority for public health research should be determining whether particles below 1 micrometer in diameter — nanoplastics — can cross cellular barriers, as larger particles are likely excreted.

The American Water Works Association, a utility trade group, said its members were reviewing the study and that existing treatment processes were designed for known contaminants, not plastic particles.
Congress has not passed legislation requiring microplastic monitoring or treatment standards; two bills addressing the issue remain in committee.
